summary: Psalm 67 begins by asking God to be merciful, bless his people, and make his face shine on them. The blessing is not pictured as private possession: the psalm asks that God's way and salvation become known among all nations, that all peoples praise God, and that the ends of the earth fear him. The chapter closes with the earth's increase and a repeated confidence that God will bless.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how praise in Psalms can move from one worshiping community to a worldwide horizon. It joins blessing, just judgment, harvest language, and the hope that all nations will recognize God.

context.author: Many writers and collections stand behind Psalms; this psalm's heading does not name an individual author.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Psalms is a five-book anthology of Hebrew poetry and prayer; Psalm 67 appears in Book II, among psalms 42-72.
context.literaryForm: A short Hebrew poem for worship, with a heading, repeated praise refrain, and two Selah markers preserved in the English text.

outline.heading: Blessing Sought
outline.note: The psalm opens with a heading and a communal request for mercy, blessing, and God's face shining on the people.

outline.heading: Known On Earth
outline.note: The requested blessing has an outward purpose: God's way and salvation would be known among all nations.

outline.heading: All Peoples Praising
outline.note: The first refrain calls the peoples, and all the peoples, to praise God.

outline.heading: Nations Glad
outline.note: The nations are invited to joy because God judges with equity and governs the nations on earth.

outline.heading: Refrain Repeated
outline.note: The praise refrain returns, keeping the psalm's worldwide focus before the reader.

outline.heading: Earth's Increase
outline.note: The earth's yield is named alongside confidence that God will bless his people.

outline.heading: Ends Of Earth
outline.note: The final line repeats the blessing and extends its result to all the ends of the earth fearing God.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. With stringed instruments. A Psalm. A song. May God be merciful to us, bless us, and cause his face to shine on us. Selah.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the psalm's setting as a worship song and states its first request: mercy, blessing, and God's favorable presence.

keyVerses.text: That your way may be known on earth, and your salvation among all nations,
keyVerses.why: This verse explains the purpose of the blessing in verse 1: God's way and salvation are to be known beyond the psalm's own community.

keyVerses.text: Oh let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you will judge the peoples with equity, and govern the nations on earth. Selah.
keyVerses.why: The psalm's worldwide praise is tied to God's just rule, not merely to Israel's private benefit.

keyVerses.text: God will bless us. All the ends of the earth shall fear him.
keyVerses.why: The closing line holds together God's blessing of the community and the recognition of God by the ends of the earth.

themes: reverence to the ends of the earth

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The speaker is communal: the psalm says “us” and “our own God.” It sounds like words for gathered worship rather than a private diary. The heading also presents it as a psalm and song for musical performance.

questions.question: What does “For the Chief Musician” tell us?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the chapter heading and points to a performance setting, but the exact ancient role is not explained in this chapter. Psalms preserves musical directions while the ancient melodies and the exact force of several performance terms are lost.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears after the opening request and again after the line about God governing the nations. Translations often preserve the Hebrew sound because its exact instruction is no longer known. In this psalm, it appears at major turns, but that placement does not establish whether it called for a pause or another performance action.

questions.question: Why does the psalm ask for blessing?
questions.answer: The blessing is requested so that God's way may be known on earth and God's salvation among all nations. The psalm does not present blessing as an end in itself. It moves from “us” to “earth,” “all nations,” “the peoples,” and “the ends of the earth.”

questions.question: Who are “the peoples” and “the nations”?
questions.answer: Within the poem, these words broaden the scene beyond the speaker's own community. The psalm calls them to praise, gladness, and joy. It also says God judges the peoples with equity and governs the nations on earth.

questions.question: Is verse 4 comforting or threatening?
questions.answer: Verse 4 presents God's judgment as a reason for the nations to be glad and sing for joy. That is because the judgment named here is “with equity,” paired with God's governing of the nations on earth. Readers may still hear judgment language differently, but in this verse it functions as good news about just rule.

questions.question: Does “The earth has yielded its increase” mean this is a harvest psalm?
questions.answer: Verse 6 uses harvest language and says the earth has produced its increase. The chapter itself does not name a festival or give a date, so it is safer to say the psalm includes harvest imagery than to assign one certain occasion. The increase becomes part of the psalm's larger confidence that God will bless.

questions.question: Why is the praise refrain repeated?
questions.answer: Verses 3 and 5 repeat the same call: “Let the peoples praise you, God. Let all the peoples praise you.” The repetition centers the chapter on worldwide praise and gives the poem a form that a congregation could easily answer or remember. Refrains suggest performance but rarely allow us to reconstruct exact ancient roles.

questions.question: What does it mean that the ends of the earth shall fear God?
questions.answer: In this psalm, fear is the final response of all the ends of the earth to God's blessing and rule. The word is not explained as panic in the chapter; it sits beside praise, gladness, joy, and recognition of God's way. A careful reading should keep those neighboring ideas in view.

glossary.def: A preserved performance marker in the psalm. Its exact ancient instruction is uncertain, so it is best read as a signal within the poem rather than translated into one firm action.
A title in the heading that points to musical or worship use. The chapter does not explain the office or role in detail.
The heading's musical direction. It tells readers the psalm was associated with instrumental performance, though the ancient melody is not preserved.
Fairness or uprightness in judgment. In this psalm, it describes how God judges the peoples.
A phrase for the farthest reaches of the earth. It completes the psalm's movement from “us” to all nations and peoples.
